body.text: In July this year, four juveniles at a juvenile observation home in Chhattisgarh’s Bilaspur escaped, allegedly after killing the watchman on duty. They were all between the ages of 18 and 20 (they were minors when placed at the observation home), and the oldest was set to be transferred to a prison after turning 21. A month later, a “security audit” of the incident produced a set of recommendations to tighten security and increase surveillance at the home.

The recommendations raised a larger question among those who have been through such incidents and their impact on juvenile homes: when a child escapes from a rehabilitation institution, should the response be more surveillance, or better rehabilitation?

The recommendations, a copy of which Frontline has seen, were submitted to Nava Raipur’s Assistant Inspector General of Police in August by the Deputy Inspector General of Police and the Senior Superintendent of Police, Bilaspur, following an audit conducted by Bilaspur’s Additional Superintendent of Police (Investigative Unit for Crime Against Women), Rashmeet Kaur Chawla.

The audit found that 98 juveniles were staying across three homes on the same premises: 56 at the observation home, 38 at the place of safety and 4 at the special home. Eighteen were above the age of 18. The institutions were operating with limited human resources: 22 contractual workers, 10 caretakers, and 2 night watchmen. For the 98 juveniles, there were 3 counsellors.

The recommendations focus heavily on physical security. They call for three Nagar Sainiks (home guards) to be stationed at the home, for the boundary wall to be raised, and for concertina wire fencing to be installed around the premises.

The most striking recommendation is the proposed expansion of CCTV surveillance: 78 cameras across the facility, 13 in the outer premises, and 65 inside. Of these, 42 are proposed for the observation home, 12 for the place of safety, and 11 for the special home. The audit also recommends increasing CCTV storage from the existing 15 days to 30 days.

The recommendations come even as the audit acknowledges a fundamental problem: overcrowding. The homes are housing more juveniles than their sanctioned capacity, and the report recommends constructing additional rooms, fitted with CCTV cameras, to accommodate them. It also recommends that the 18 juveniles who have crossed the age of 18 be transferred elsewhere.
Rehabilitation takes a back seat

The audit does not identify a need for psychological counselling. It does, however, identify a need for legal counselling for children in conflict with law, so that they understand the proceedings against them and can work towards improving their behaviour.

The gap between the resources proposed for surveillance and those available for rehabilitation is stark: for 98 children, 3 counsellors. Juvenile justice experts say this imbalance reflects a deeper misreading of what such institutions are for. “Think why a juvenile will run away from reform,” said Ashok Tangde, a child rights expert based in Beed, Maharashtra. “Even if they are escaping, stop them through counselling and by understanding their needs, not through police forces and surveillance.”

Tangde questioned the assumption that an escape necessarily points to a need for stronger physical security. “They are not culprits; the system prepares them to be one,” he said. “If someone is getting food on time, why would they need to steal it?”

According to him, authorities often treat an escape primarily as a security failure rather than examining why a child wanted to leave the institution in the first place. “Just because the authorities can’t reform them or understand them, they bring in the police,” he said, arguing that children in conflict with law need to be approached in a manner suited to their age and circumstances.

The Juvenile Justice Act deliberately does not describe these children as criminals; they are termed “children in conflict with law,” a distinction that reflects the rehabilitative philosophy of juvenile justice.

The terminology around these institutions has evolved too. What were once called “correction homes” or “supervision homes” are now institutions governed under the juvenile justice framework. The three years a child may spend in such an institution is meant to facilitate care, protection, and rehabilitation, not punishment.

Yet Tangde argues that the institutional response to an escape increasingly moves in the opposite direction. He also questioned whether extensive CCTV surveillance could itself undermine rehabilitation. “This massive surveillance through CCTVs would add to their curiosity. They would find ways to get past it, and it would not help them reform,” he said.

Authorities have their own explanation for the emphasis on surveillance. Frontline asked officials why extensive CCTV monitoring was considered necessary, and whether the institutions could function without such measures.

A warden at a juvenile home in Haryana, speaking on condition of anonymity, pointed to incidents of juveniles turning ordinary objects into weapons. “The juveniles were given spoons, but they transformed them into knives,” she said. Pipes beneath washbasins had to be removed too, she said, because juveniles would cut them into sharp weapons.

For the warden, such incidents make CCTV surveillance necessary. But surveillance also has obvious limits. What happens if two juveniles use their hands to assault each other? What if one attempts to choke another? How far can surveillance reasonably extend inside an institution meant to provide care and rehabilitation? When Frontline asked the warden whether sustained counselling and rehabilitation might offer a more effective and durable solution, she agreed.
A pattern beyond Bilaspur
The response in Bilaspur is not an isolated one. Across juvenile institutions, security measures tend to tighten after escape attempts.

In Jaipur, Rajasthan, home guards have been stationed at the entry gates of dormitories, and police personnel deployed outside the facility, after some juveniles reportedly broke through an already dilapidated wall and attempted to escape in 2024. The pattern is telling: an escape brings tighter walls, more guards and greater surveillance, while the reasons that prompted the escape receive comparatively little attention.

The resources directed towards surveillance also raise questions about how much funding remains for care and rehabilitation at juvenile homes. A caretaker at a juvenile home in Rajasthan told Frontline that under Mission Vatsalya, caretakers and counsellors are paid Rs.14,564 and Rs.23,170 a month respectively, while home guards deployed by the state typically earn Rs.28,950 a month.

The cost of installing and maintaining CCTV cameras adds a further recurring expense. “The state always says there is a budget constraint. They cannot increase our pay, but they have money for all this,” the caretaker said.
How surveillance entered juvenile homes

The shift towards surveillance has a legal history, traceable to the 2016 amendments to the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Model Rules. Rule 67 introduced “security measures” and recognised “risk to and from the child” as a security concern, enabling CCTV cameras at key points, including dormitories, corridors, and the entry and exit points of washrooms.

This marked a departure from the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Rules, 2007, which primarily recognised the abuse and exploitation of the child at the hands of those responsible for their care and protection under Rule 60 and permitted CCTV cameras only at the entrance of the premises, not within children’s living spaces.

The 2016 framework did not abandon child protection: it continued to recognise abuse and exploitation of the child under Rule 76. But it also introduced a parallel emphasis on securing institutions against risks posed by, or to, children. The question is what has happened to that balance in practice. As surveillance expands, has security begun to take precedence over protection and rehabilitation?

The change represents more than an administrative decision to install cameras. It reflects a shift in how children in conflict with law are perceived within these institutions: from children requiring protection and rehabilitation to children who themselves constitute a security risk. That shift sits uneasily with the central philosophy of the Juvenile Justice Act, which places the best interests of the child at its core.
Yet, even as surveillance is increasingly being presented as central to security in juvenile homes, there is little systematic data on either the number of escapes or the extent of CCTV coverage.

“There is no data maintained about how many juveniles escaped the homes. It just comes out in the news whenever and wherever it happens. The rules mention placing CCTVs in the homes but there is no clarification on its number as such,” an official at the Department of Child Rights in Jaipur told Frontline on condition of anonymity.

The absence of such data makes it difficult to assess patterns of escape, identify recurring security gaps, or determine whether measures introduced after incidents have actually worked. Surveillance, therefore, risks becoming a reactive response to individual incidents rather than part of a data-driven security strategy.

A juvenile home is not meant to be a prison with younger inmates. Its walls are meant to protect children, not contain them. Yet as security measures multiply, from CCTV cameras and fencing to guards and surveillance, these homes risk becoming spaces where control takes precedence over care, and preventing escape overshadows the purpose of rehabilitation. The question, then, is not whether institutions need security. It is what happens when security becomes the answer to every failure of rehabilitation.

The juveniles who escaped the Bilaspur Juvenile Home are yet to be apprehended. The authorities are not willing to speak. When asked about the logic behind this massive surveillance, Sujata Haldar, superintendent at the juvenile observation home in Bilaspur, told Frontline that they don’t speak to journalists about anything related to juveniles.

In the case of the juveniles who escaped from the Bilaspur juvenile home, news reports said that they allegedly took away the digital video recorder (DVR) connected to the CCTV cameras, purportedly to destroy evidence. The allegation itself remains to be established. There is, as of yet, no substantial evidence to conclude that the juveniles were responsible for the murder that preceded the escape.

But the incident has set in motion a revealing chain of responses. The alleged removal of the DVR—whether or not the juveniles were responsible for the crime—has reinforced the institutional impulse to respond to insecurity with more surveillance. Cameras, recording systems, higher walls, fencing and additional security personnel are increasingly becoming the visible markers of a “secure” juvenile home.

A juvenile home is not meant to function merely as a secured enclosure. Under the juvenile justice framework, security is meant to coexist with care, rehabilitation and reintegration. Yet, in the aftermath of incidents such as Bilaspur, surveillance can become an easier and more tangible response than investing in counsellors, meaningful engagement, education and individualised rehabilitation.

Bilaspur offers a starting point for investigating that shift: as juvenile homes become more heavily surveilled, are they also becoming better equipped to rehabilitate the children placed inside them?
Shruti Jain is an independent journalist and researcher based in Gurugram
